Maladaptive Strategies.value: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

vignette: Thirty years ago, Clara was ambushed in her kitchen while preparing dinner. The assailant had pinned her against the counter, his hands gripping her neck and wrists with bruising force while he demanded she recount the details of the assault in real time. That forced narration and the physical focus on her neck and arms forged a direct line to her present-day vulnerabilities; whenever a conversation turned toward their future plans or she caught sight of her own hands resting on the table, the memories would rush back, unbidden and visceral. In the months that followed, her belief that she was fundamentally inadequate to process the trauma actively fractured how the past surfaced, ensuring that the recollections would either spike with uncontainable rage or slip into a cold, detached numbness before she could fully grasp them. Because she was certain she could not handle the thoughts, she leaned into her routines of avoidance, further restricting her intake of food and doubling down on her refusal to exercise. When the recollections surfaced, bringing either a burning fury or a hollow detachment, she would immediately retreat into her established defenses, forcing her spine against the drywall and skipping meals until the sensation passed. Each time a fragment of the assault breached her conscious mind, it fed her conviction that she was incapable of healing, eroding the happiness she once took for granted and cementing her sense of inadequacy. By the time she returned to her work as a forensic analyst, the maintaining cycle had solidified into her daily routine. Her profession demanded meticulous attention to physical evidence, yet her constant habit of sitting with her back to the wall and starving herself slowly drained the emotional texture from her recollections, leaving her able to remember the sequence of events only as if she were watching a stranger’s life unfold. This emotional flattening paradoxically made her more susceptible to external cues; the unresolved nature of the recollections acted as a magnet for stimuli, making the sight of her own neck in the mirror or a simple discussion of the event itself spark renewed distress. The isolation fostered by her avoidance behaviors left her hyper-vigilant in empty rooms, so that even a passing reference to the past would jolt her into a state of heightened alertness. By physically withdrawing and denying her body what it needed, she convinced herself that her capacity for joy had been permanently severed. Her husband’s attempts to engage her in weekend plans now felt like taunts, because the belief that she was broken by the experience amplified the threat of everyday stimuli, turning casual remarks about tomorrow into immediate alarms. The cumulative toll eventually fractured her professional life. During a recent case review, the weight of her internal state became undeniable when she sat across from a witness who began describing the assault. As the man spoke, the conversation about the event triggered a wave of blocked memory and physiological rage, forcing Clara to abruptly close the case files and excuse herself. She realized her analytical sharpness had dulled, not from age, but from the exhausting arithmetic of staying vigilant, starving herself, and retreating from any forward-looking conversation. At seventy-one, what finally brought her to the clinic was not the passage of time, but a sudden, terrifying realization that she could no longer tolerate the silence she had built around herself. She hoped for a way to quiet the rage without starving, to look toward the future without bracing for impact, and to finally believe that she was more than just inadequate to survive her past.
